messages.subject: Re: Nimble MCMC algorithm no working with Conway Maxwell Poisson Distribution
messages.subject_clean: Nimble MCMC algorithm no working with Conway Maxwell Poisson Distribution
messages.body_plain:
Lokesh, thanks for your use of NIMBLE.  I'm not quite sure what the problem you were having was.  I provided initial values to the model, so that the first model build was "fully initialized", which I think is always a good idea.  Then I continued with your mechanism of generating data (which turns out to be the same: all 1's), and using that.

Then, I also broke down the MCMC building into the separate steps of configuration, then building, so we can inspect the MCMC itself.  I think this is *always* a useful intermediate step, so you know what's actually going on in the MCMC, and can catch if something (usually in the samplers) seems amiss.

Everything compiled and ran fine.  You'll definitely want to do longer MCMC runs (I lowered it to 1000 iterations), but the MCMC seems to get started fine.

You might consider using the runMCMC() function, rather than mcmc$run(), but either will work fine.

You might also check out the samplesPlot() function, provided in the package basicMCMCplots.  I used it in the code below.

Let us know if you're still having problems here.  All my code is copied below.  Most of my comments that I added are proceeded by "DT"

Cheers!
Daniel

library(CompGLM)
library(nimble)

ZICMPcode <- nimbleCode({
    p~dunif(0,1)
    lam~dunif(0,100)
    nu~dunif(0,100)
    for(i in 1:N) {
        y[i] ~ dZICMP(lam, nu,sumTo = 200L,zeroProb = p)
    }
})

## constants, data, and initial values
constants <- list(N = 100)

dCMP <- nimbleRcall(function(y = integer(), lam = double(), nu = double(),sumTo = integer(),logP = logical(0, default = 0)){}, Rfun = 'dcomp',

                    returnType = double() )##  DT: shouldn't need this: envir = .GlobalEnv)

rCMP <- nimbleRcall(function(n = integer(), lam = double(), nu = double(),sumTo = integer()){}, Rfun = 'rcomp',

                    returnType = integer()) ## DT: shouldn't need this: envir = .GlobalEnv)

dZICMP <- nimbleFunction(
    run = function(x = integer(), lam = double(), nu = double(),sumTo = integer(), zeroProb = double(), log = logical(0, default = 0)) {
        returnType(double())
        ## First handle non-zero data
        if(x != 0) {
            ## return the log probability if log = TRUE
            if(log) return(dCMP(x, lam, nu,sumTo = 200L, log = TRUE) + log(1-zeroProb))
            ## or the probability if log = FALSE
            else return((1-zeroProb) * dCMP(x, lam, nu,sumTo = 200L, log = FALSE))
        }
        ## From here down we know x is 0
        totalProbZero <- zeroProb + (1-zeroProb) * dCMP(0, lam, nu,sumTo = 200L, log = FALSE)
        if(log) return(log(totalProbZero))
        return(totalProbZero)
    })

rZICMP <- nimbleFunction(
    run = function(n = integer(), lam = double(), nu = double(),sumTo = integer(), zeroProb = double()) {
        returnType(integer())
        isStructuralZero <- rbinom(1, prob = zeroProb, size = 1)
        if(isStructuralZero) return(0)
        return(rCMP(1, lam,nu,sumTo = 200L))
    })

registerDistributions(list(
    dZICMP = list(
        BUGSdist = "dZICMP(lam, nu,sumTo, zeroProb)",
        discrete = TRUE,
        range = c(0, Inf),
        types = c('value = integer()', 'lam = double()', 'nu = double()','sumTo = integer()', 'zeroProb = double()')
    )))

## DT: let's include the model check.
## it's helpful, especially for such a small model:
ZICMPmodel <- nimbleModel( ZICMPcode, constants=constants) ##check = FALSE)

ZICMPmodel$calculate()   ## something is wrong here!
## DT:
## Error in if (x != 0) { : missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
## looks like since we're missing values for y[i] (no initial values were provided)
## this first logical if() statement in your dZICMP() function definition
## is failing.  Let's provide initial values and try again:

inits <- list(p = 0.5,
              lam = 1,
              nu = 1)

data <- list(y = rep(1, constants$N))

ZICMPmodel <- nimbleModel( ZICMPcode, constants=constants, data=data, inits=inits)

ZICMPmodel$calculate()    ## -178.5251    DT: that's better

ZICMPmodel$p <- .4
ZICMPmodel$lam <- 1.8
ZICMPmodel$nu<-0.9
ZICMPmodel$simulate('y')

ZICMPmodel$calculate()    ##  -191.4907    DT: still good

simulatedData <- ZICMPmodel$y
simulatedData
hist(simulatedData)

ZICMPmodel$setData(list(y = simulatedData))
cZICMPmodel <- compileNimble(ZICMPmodel)

## DT: let's configure the MCMC first, look at the samplers
## that are assigned, and the monitors.  Always
## helpful and a good idea to know what's going on in the MCMC:
##ZICMPmcmc <- buildMCMC(ZICMPmodel)   not this line, but instead:

conf <- configureMCMC(ZICMPmodel)

conf$printMonitors()
## thin = 1: p, lam, nu

conf$printSamplers()
## [1] RW sampler: p
## [2] RW sampler: lam
## [3] RW sampler: nu

## DT: now build the MCMC, and compile it:
ZICMPmcmc <- buildMCMC(conf)

cZICMPmcmc <- compileNimble(ZICMPmcmc, project = ZICMPmodel)

cZICMPmcmc$run(1000)   ## using fewer iterations

samples <- as.matrix(cZICMPmcmc$mvSamples)

samplesSummary(samples)
##           Mean      Median    St.Dev.    95%CI_low  95%CI_upp
## lam 0.62186699 0.560347129 0.18223126 0.4068033525 0.93935815
## nu  0.34242280 0.014943882 0.40012792 0.0026253462 0.90000000
## p   0.02232572 0.002589668 0.02716132 0.0009254903 0.05182992

library(basicMCMCplots)
samplesPlot(samples)    ## DT: looks like we need longer runs, but things are off to a good start

messages.subject: Box Cox transformation
messages.subject_clean: Box Cox transformation
messages.body_plain:
Hi
I'm doing a project for bayesian inference based box-cox transformation data. I define a box-cox transformation function with nimble function, and give priors on box-cox transformation parameter lambda, and use loglikelihood control the sampling. The code cannot be complied into C++. I attached the code in this email. I think it is something wrong with boxcox transfomation code. Could you help me with this problem?
Best
Guanyu

boxcox<- nimbleFunction(
  run=function(raw=double(1),lambda=double(1),constant=double(1)){
    returnType(double(1))
    if (lambda == 0) {
      return(log(raw - constant))
    } else {
      return(((raw - constant) ^ lambda - 1) / (lambda))
    }
  })

boxcoxfit<- nimbleCode({
  for (i in 1:n){
    y_star[i]<- boxcox(y[i],lambda,constant)
    mu[i]<-beta0+beta1*x1[i]+beta2*x2[i]+beta3*x3[i]
    #y_star[i]~dnorm(mu[i],var=sigma2)
    logll[i]<-0.5*log(2*3.14)-0.5*log(sigma2)-1/sigma2*pow((y_star[i]-mu[i]),2)
  }
  ll<-sum(logll[1:n])
  sigma2~dinvgamma(1,1)
  beta0~dnorm(0,sd=10)
  beta1~dnorm(0,sd=10)
  beta2~dnorm(0,sd=10)
  beta3~dnorm(0,sd=10)
  lambda~dnorm(0,sd=10)
})
llFun <- nimbleFunction(
  setup <- function(model) {},

  run <- function() {
    ll<-model$ll
    returnType(double())
    return(ll[1])
  }
)
n=100
y=rnorm(100,0,1)
x1=rnorm(100,0,1)
x2=rnorm(100,0,1)
x3=rnorm(100,0,1)

data <- list(
  y =y ,x1=x1,x2=x2,x3=x3
)
constants <- list(
  n = n,constant=-10
)
inits <- list(lambda=0,sigma2=1,beta0=1,beta1=1,beta2=1,beta3=1)

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(boxcoxfit, data = data, constants = constants,inits=inits)

RllFun <- llFun(Rmodel)
mcmcConf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, nodes = NULL)
mcmcConf$addMonitors(target = c("beta0","beta1", "beta2", "beta3", "sigma2","lambda"))
mcmcConf$addSampler(target = "beta0", type = 'RW_llFunction',
                   control = list(llFunction = RllFun,
                                  includesTarget = FALSE))

mcmcConf$addSampler(target = "beta1", type = 'RW_llFunction',
                    control = list(llFunction = RllFun,
                                   includesTarget = FALSE))

mcmcConf$addSampler(target = "beta2", type = 'RW_llFunction',
                    control = list(llFunction = RllFun,
                                   includesTarget = FALSE))

mcmcConf$addSampler(target = "beta3", type = 'RW_llFunction',
                    control = list(llFunction = RllFun,
                                   includesTarget = FALSE))

mcmcConf$addSampler(target = "sigma2", type = 'RW_llFunction',
                    control = list(llFunction = RllFun,
                                   includesTarget = FALSE))

mcmcConf$addSampler(target = "lambda", type = 'RW_llFunction',
                    control = list(llFunction = RllFun,
                                   includesTarget = FALSE))

Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(mcmcConf)
Cmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel)
## MCMC run
Cmcmc$run(1000)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Guanyu,

It looks like there are some problems with the dimensions in your
boxcox() function and in your model.
You specify that 'raw', 'lambda', and 'constant' are all vectors in
your nimbleFunction arguments but then
you use 'lambda' as a scalar. Also, in the model, all three of them
are scalars even though they are passed
in to the boxcox() function.

Note that if you run printErrors() after getting a compilation error,
you can often get useful information
that would guide you in determining what the problem is.

As a side note, it might be more straightforward to create a
user-defined boxcox distribution rather than
using the "RW_llFunction" sampler and let NIMBLE choose what sampler
to use (or you could
override NIMBLE's default and choose a different sampler, such as a
slice sampler). But it's up to you.

Chris

messages.body_plain:
hi Guanyu, I'm still not sure that I fully understand.

Is the idea that you have (in BUGS-like syntax)

for(i in 1:n)
 y[i] ~ dnorm(x[i]*beta + w[i], var = sigma2)

and you want w[i] to be specified nonparametrically and you want to
allow a box-cox transformation of y?

If so, in order to use the dCRP distribution to have w[i] be
nonparametric as discussed in the NIMBLE manual,
you will need to allow NIMBLE to place its special sampler on the
vector of cluster indicators in the DP mixture
representation.

So I think the thing to do is to implement the box-cox transformation
as a user-defined distribution rather than using the RW_llfunction,
and then allow NIMBLE to choose the samplers to use for the model parameters.

Chris

Dear Hamze,

In general, 500 dimensions shouldn't be a problem.  People often write models with thousands of dimensions for MCMC sampling due to many latent states.

Performance of samplers really depends on the model and the data.  A good strategy would be to see how nimble's default samplers do and then decide if improving performance is worth your effort.

-Perry

messages.subject_clean: support for NAs in multivariate distributions
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to the developers and countless contributors for all the great work building this useful software.

In the Nimble User Manual version 0.7.1 it is noted in Section 6.1.1.3 concerning missing data values that "A node following a multivariate distribution must be either entirely observed or entirely missing."

Is there any planned support for partially observed multivariate distributions? In particular, for multivariate Gaussian-distributed random variables?

Thanks very much,
Henry

In the Nimble User Manual version 0.7.1 it is noted in Section 6.1.1.3 concerning missin

messages.subject: Re: support for NAs in multivariate distributions
messages.subject_clean: support for NAs in multivariate distributions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Henry, good question, and thanks for weighing in with feature
requests - it's always helpful to know what users might want to do.

We don't have any plans at the moment for supporting this formally
given various other priorities, but you can at the moment already do
this.

You can work around the system slightly as in the following simple
example, which hopefully
is close enough to what you want to do to give you the idea.

y <- c(NA, 2)
yMiss <- is.na <http://is.na>(y)
y[yMiss] <- rnorm(sum(is.na <http://is.na>(y)))  # initialize missing values
code <- nimbleCode({
    y[1:2] ~ dmnorm(mu[1:2], pr[1:2,1:2])
    mu[1:2] ~ dmnorm(z[1:2],pr[1:2,1:2])
})
m <- nimbleModel(code, data = list(y = y),
                 inits = list(z = rep(0,2), pr=diag(2)))
conf <- configureMCMC(m)
m$isData('y')  # TRUE
for(i in seq_along(yMiss))
    if(yMiss[i]) conf$addSampler(paste0('y[', i, ']'),'RW')  # or
slice or some other sampler
conf$printSamplers()
# [1] conjugate_dmnorm_dmnorm sampler: mu[1:2]
# [2] RW sampler: y[1]

A few comments:

0) NIMBLE considers things to be 'data' at the level of the node so
y[1:p] in its entirety is considered either
data or not, hence the note in the user manual.

1) You need to provide the data without any NAs when running
nimbleModel; otherwise nimble will
not flag 'y' as 'data' and will assign a multivariate sampler to the
entire vector that overwrites the
actual fixed data values.  Also, by providing
non-NA values, you are initializing the missing data elements. Usually
if NAs are provided this would
be done if necessary by the MCMC but since 'y' is flagged as 'data',
NIMBLE's MCMC initialization
will not simulate into those values.

2) Note that if 'y' is long, this will be computationally inefficient
because the scalar sampling for each element of 'y' will
have to do the full multivariate normal density calculations since NIMBLE
does not know how to break down a multivariate normal into blocks and
condition one block on the other.

3a) For more efficiency, you could write a user-defined sampler for
the missing 'y's conditional on the available 'y's where you
code up the conditional density calculations. If you do this, you
might share it with the user group as that
might well be useful for others. This is something that the
development team can think about adding to NIMBLE.

3b) Alternatively, simply assigning a block sampler to the missing
'y's would avoid some of the inefficiency as well,
though it would still be doing a full multivariate density calculation
for the entire vector of 'y's.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
I appreciate the development of NIMBLE and it is a great tool. I am having some difficulty in running a dcar_proper model with my full dataset.  In my case, NIMBLE freezes after:

“running calculate on model (any error reports that follow may simply reflect missing values in model variables) ...”

I used the USGS Adjacency For WinBUGS Tool to extract the neighbor adjacency structure for my dataset. My dataset is on a stream network and consists of 86 sites with between 16 and 50+ reaches (~100m in length) at each site. This is referred to as the full dataset and includes all 1628 reaches (pres_num_adj.csv). In the simplest case for a site, there are 8 reaches for fish presence immediately followed by 8 fish absence reaches upstream. I plan to use GIS attributes (gradient, flow, etc.) to model the upper most occurrence of salmon in a stream using CAR models.  Because of this design the autocorrelation is over 95% between adjacent reaches. Not having done this before, I used the CAR examples in the NIMBLE manual to better understand these models and the code.  I followed up with ICAR and CAR proper model using my data with no covariates to develop models and will eventually follow up with covariate models.

I created a second dataset is pres_num_adj_short.csv, which includes the first 3 sites with 96 reaches and the associated presence data, number of adjacent reaches, and the numbered reaches associated with adjacency count.

The ICAR model with no covariates runs on both datasets.  The second model is a CAR proper model. I used the first parameterization in the NIMBLE manual (e.g. not specifying C and M). The car proper model runs on the “short’ dataset but will not run on the full dataset and freezes after “running calculate on model (any error reports that follow may simply reflect missing values in model variables) ...”

I have checked the data structure in the csv files and it seems appropriate. I am using NIMBLE VERSION 0.7.0. I have used the latest R version and 3.4.4.  I have used Rstudio and directly run NIMBLE through the R GUI.  Despite all of this the problem still persist for the full dataset for the CAR proper model.

Any suggestions would be appreciated and I would be happy to send you the code and data if that helps.  Thanks for considering this request.

Dan

messages.subject_clean: NIMBLE freezes using dcar_proper model
messages.body_plain:
Dan, thanks for posting your question, and also for following up separately, off-list, to share your model and data set so we could diagnose the problem you're experiencing.

As it turns out, the underlying library we use for matrix algebra (the Eigen C++ package) appears to *not* handle your particular spatial adjacency structure very well.  Specifically, when the NIMBLE model object is constructed, under-the-hood NIMBLE reparameterizes your model to our "canonical" parameterization, which has the advantage of pre-calculating some fixed constants (based up the spatial adjacency structure), which will then be immediately available for use during the course of MCMC sampling (and will never need to be re-calculated again).  The canonical parameterization for the CAR proper distribution is takes the form:

s[1:N] ~ dcar_proper(mu, C, adj, num, M, tau, gamma, evs)

where "C", "M", and "evs" are deterministically calculated from the "adj" and "num" vectors.

The specific problem comes from generating "evs", which is the vector of N eigenvalues of an intermediate NxN matrix.  It's during that eigen decomposition of this matrix, being done by the Eigen C++ library, that appears to scale very poorly for your particular adjacency structure, and appears to "hang", as it never seems to finish the computation.

I have two alternate paths forward for you, either of which should work:

Option 1. Oddly, R's native eigen() decomposition functionality appears to work fine for your model.  So, getting around this problem is as easy as doing these pre-calculations yourself in R (which will use R's eigen() function, which appears to work fine for your spatial structure), then parameterizing your proper CAR distribution as shown above, and additionally providing the (pre-calculated) "C", "M", and "evs" values through the "constants" list for creating your model.  Thus, your modified code would look something like:

C <- nimble::CAR_calcC(adj, num)
M <- nimble::CAR_calcM(num)
Cmatrix <- nimble::CAR_calcCmatrix(C, adj, num)
evs <- eigen(Cmatrix, only.values = TRUE)$values    ## using R's eigen()

## old constants list:
##constants <- list(adj=adj, num=num, L=L, N=N)

## new constants list:
constants <- list(adj=adj, num=num, L=L, N=N, C=C, M=M, evs=evs)

code <- nimbleCode({
    ...
    ## new dcar_proper parametization:
    s[1:N] ~ dcar_proper(mu[1:N], C=C[1:L], adj=adj[1:L], num=num[1:N], M=M[1:N], tau=tau, gamma=gamma, evs=evs[1:N])
    ...
})

## define "data", and "inits", the same as you already are

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code, constants, data, inits)

This construction of the model, already having pre-calculated "evs" yourself in R, should work fine, and can be carried through to building an MCMC, compilation, and running the compiled MCMC.

Option 2: It also appears to be the case that the Eigen C++ library is able to handle the eigen decomposition fine, if we only request the eigen *values* (since that's all we need), and not the eigen *vectors*.  So, I've made this change to the underlying NIMBLE code for the proper CAR distribution, to only calculate the eigen *values*.  Using this approach, it finishes in a reasonably short time.  I've made these changes, and pushed them to the development branch of nimble ("devel"), which you can install using:

remove.packages('nimble')
library(devtools)
install_github('nimble-dev/nimble', ref = 'devel', subdir = 'packages/nimble')
library(nimble)

Once you have the updated package installed, your original code that you were using should work fine.  (And give, literally, identical calculations and inferences to Option 1 above).  So, it's up to you if you want to install this updated version of nimble, or to re-parameterize your model slightly.  Also, this change in the development branch will be included in our next release of the nimble package, whenever that is.

I hope this sorts it out, but please keep in touch with any other questions.

Cheers!
Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hi Lokesh,

Thanks for making an example with more informative data, so it's more clear that there is a real sampling problem.

I think this is revealing a bug related to nimbleRcall and R's garbage collection, which is creating incorrect values being passed from C++ to R or back.  We have seen a bug related to this previously, which we fixed, but evidently there is more to it.  I think it has to do with use of PROTECT in C++ code for R.

What convinces me that something like this is the problem is that I was able to write dcomp purely as a nimbleFunction, so that no nimbleRcall is needed, and now the results look reasonable.  To write it this way, I looked at the CompGLM C++ source code, where I saw that the functions dcomp and Z were both easy to write as nimbleFunctions.

Using the following pieces makes it work for me.  I hope this gets you under way on your goal, while we take longer to figure out what the problem with nimbleRcall is.

calcZ <- nimbleFunction(
    run = function(lam = double(), nu = double(), sumTo = double()) {
        ## CompGLM C++ source code:
        ##         double Z(double lam, double nu, int sumTo) {
        ##  double sum = 1.0;
        ##  double factorial = 1.0;
        ##  double lamPower = lam;
        ##  for (int i = 1; i <= sumTo; ++i) {
        ##  factorial *= i;
        ##  sum += lamPower / pow(factorial, nu);
        ##  lamPower *= lam;
        ##  }
        ##  return sum;
        ## }
        sum <- 1
        factorial <- 1
        lamPower <- lam
        for(i in 1:sumTo) {
            factorial <- factorial * i
            sum <- sum + lamPower / pow(factorial, nu)
            lamPower <- lamPower * lam
        }
        return(sum)
        returnType(double())
    }
)

dCMP_nf <- nimbleFunction(
    ## Normally a dist random variable must be called x, but this is not really the dist function being called, so the name "y" will work
    run = function(y = double(), lam = double(), nu = double(), sumTo = double(), log = integer(0, default = 0) ) {
        ## C source code from package CompGLM (which is wrapped by another layer that handles log):
        ##         double dcomp(int y, double lam, double nu, int sumTo) {
        ##  if (y < 0) {
        ##  return 0.0;
        ##  } else {
        ##  return pow(lam, y) / (pow(factorial(y), nu) * Z(lam, nu, sumTo));
        ##  }
        ## }
        returnType(double())
        if(y < 0) {
            if(log) return(-Inf)
            else return(0)
        } else {
            prob <- pow(lam, y) / (pow(factorial(y), nu) * calcZ(lam, nu, sumTo))
            if(log) return(log(prob))
            else return(prob)
        }
    }
)

dZICMP <- nimbleFunction(
    run = function(x = integer(), lam = double(), nu = double(),sumTo = integer(), zeroProb = double(), log = logical(0, default = 0)) {
        returnType(double())

##        print("x = ", x, " lam = ", lam, " nu = ", nu, " zeroProb = ", zeroProb)

        ## First handle non-zero data
        if(x != 0) {
            ## return the log probability if log = TRUE

            if(log) return(dCMP_nf(x, lam, nu,sumTo = 200L, log = TRUE) + log(1-zeroProb))

            ## or the probability if log = FALSE

            else return((1-zeroProb) * dCMP_nf(x, lam, nu,sumTo = 200L, log = FALSE))

        }
        ## From here down we know x is 0

        totalProbZero <- zeroProb + (1-zeroProb) * dCMP_nf(0, lam, nu,sumTo = 200L, log = FALSE)
        if(log) return(log(totalProbZero))
        return(totalProbZero)
    })

Thank you so much pdevalpine.

It finally worked.

On Friday, April 12, 2019 at 11:49:30 PM UTC+5:30, pdevalpine wrote:

> Hi Lokesh,
>
> Thanks for making an example with more informative data, so it's more clear that there is a real sampling problem.
>
> I think this is revealing a bug related to nimbleRcall and R's garbage collection, which is creating incorrect values being passed from C++ to R or back.  We have seen a bug related to this previously, which we fixed, but evidently there is more to it.  I think it has to do with use of PROTECT in C++ code for R.
>
> What convinces me that something like this is the problem is that I was able to write dcomp purely as a nimbleFunction, so that no nimbleRcall is needed, and now the results look reasonable.  To write it this way, I looked at the CompGLM C++ source code, where I saw that the functions dcomp and Z were both easy to write as nimbleFunctions.
>
> Using the following pieces makes it work for me.  I hope this gets you under way on your goal, while we take longer to figure out what the problem with nimbleRcall is.
>
> calcZ <- nimbleFunction(
>     run = function(lam = double(), nu = double(), sumTo = double()) {
>         ## CompGLM C++ source code:
>         ##         double Z(double lam, double nu, int sumTo) {
>         ##  double sum = 1.0;
>         ##  double factorial = 1.0;
>         ##  double lamPower = lam;
>         ##  for (int i = 1; i <= sumTo; ++i) {
>         ##  factorial *= i;
>         ##  sum += lamPower / pow(factorial, nu);
>         ##  lamPower *= lam;
>         ##  }
>         ##  return sum;
>         ## }
>         sum <- 1
>         factorial <- 1
>         lamPower <- lam
>         for(i in 1:sumTo) {
>             factorial <- factorial * i
>             sum <- sum + lamPower / pow(factorial, nu)
>             lamPower <- lamPower * lam
>         }
>         return(sum)
>         returnType(double())
>     }
> )
>
> dCMP_nf <- nimbleFunction(
>     ## Normally a dist random variable must be called x, but this is not really the dist function being called, so the name "y" will work
>     run = function(y = double(), lam = double(), nu = double(), sumTo = double(), log = integer(0, default = 0) ) {
>         ## C source code from package CompGLM (which is wrapped by another layer that handles log):
>         ##         double dcomp(int y, double lam, double nu, int sumTo) {
>         ##  if (y < 0) {
>         ##  return 0.0;
>         ##  } else {
>         ##  return pow(lam, y) / (pow(factorial(y), nu) * Z(lam, nu, sumTo));
>         ##  }
>         ## }
>         returnType(double())
>         if(y < 0) {
>             if(log) return(-Inf)
>             else return(0)
>         } else {
>             prob <- pow(lam, y) / (pow(factorial(y), nu) * calcZ(lam, nu, sumTo))
>             if(log) return(log(prob))
>             else return(prob)
>         }
>     }
> )
>
> dZICMP <- nimbleFunction(
>     run = function(x = integer(), lam = double(), nu = double(),sumTo = integer(), zeroProb = double(), log = logical(0, default = 0)) {
>         returnType(double())
> ##        print("x = ", x, " lam = ", lam, " nu = ", nu, " zeroProb = ", zeroProb)
>         ## First handle non-zero data
>         if(x != 0) {
>             ## return the log probability if log = TRUE
>             if(log) return(dCMP_nf(x, lam, nu,sumTo = 200L, log = TRUE) + log(1-zeroProb))
>             ## or the probability if log = FALSE
>             else return((1-zeroProb) * dCMP_nf(x, lam, nu,sumTo = 200L, log = FALSE))
>         }
>         ## From here down we know x is 0
>         totalProbZero <- zeroProb + (1-zeroProb) * dCMP_nf(0, lam, nu,sumTo = 200L, log = FALSE)
>         if(log) return(log(totalProbZero))
>         return(totalProbZero)
>     })
>
>
>

  alpha0 ~ dnorm(0,sd = 10000)

messages.body_plain:
I don't think you need rCMP_nf to work.  If you want it to work, a quick guess is that "break" is the problem.  When you define the nimbleFunction, there is a warning message about break.  That is telling you that it may not compile unless it is going to be defined as a nimbleFunction later (and actually, in this case, it is not even a function call).  I think you could replace "break" with "return(sample)".

For MCEM, you may need to provide box constraints for the optimization(s).  You could run it uncompiled and trap the warnings or inspect the model variables and log probabilities after it breaks.  Or the model might just not be initialized well.  Did you try calculating the whole model?  You can access model variables and log probabilities and calculate parts of the model in order to track down where there is a problem.

It's a hasty answer at the end of the day in my time zone, but I hope it helps.

messages.subject: Model compilation problems
messages.subject_clean: Model compilation problems
messages.body_plain:
Hey all,
I am having a weird compilation error. I say weird, because my colleague
was able to compile and run this model on his machine (linux,mint), while I
have been consistently getting the same error on my own 2 computers (linux,
ubuntu). Currently I have the latest nimble-dev version installed re: drfishes
from this user list and using R 3.5.3.

I have written a nimble function to calculate derived quantities, then pass
these quantities back to the model to be used in the likelihood.
The R function runs as expected. I can compile the R function, and it also runs as expected (same outcomes, faster).
When I try to compile the nimble model that uses the nimble function, I get an error:

Error: Failed to create the shared library.

The end of the compileNimble output with a failure message:
/usr/lib/R/etc/Makeconf:172: recipe for target 'P_6_modelcode_MID_5_nfCode.o' failed
P_6_modelcode_MID_5_nfCode.cpp: In member function ‘virtual void p_L5_UID_50::simulate(const ind

#nimblefunction
state.transition<- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(records = integer(0),
                 beta0 = double(0),
                 agem=integer(1),
                 Nage_lookup=integer(0),
                 car_age=double(1),
                 age_lookup=integer(1)) {
    p <- nimNumeric(records)
    gam <-nimMatrix(value = 0,nrow = records,ncol =Nage_lookup )
    for (i in 1:records) {
      for (k in 1:agem[i]) {
        gam[i,k]<-beta0 +  car_age[age_lookup[k]]
      }
    p[i] <- 1-exp(-sum(exp(gam[i,1:agem[i]])))
    }
    returnType(double(1))
    return(p[1:records])
  })

Cstate.transition <- compileNimble(state.transition,showCompilerOutput = TRUE) #runs and compiles okay

#nimblemodel
modelcode <- nimbleCode({
  prec  ~ dgamma(0.01, 0.01)
  beta0 ~ T(dnorm(-6,3),-9,-1)
  for (i in 1:Tage) {car_age[i] ~ dnorm(0,prec)  }

  p[1:records]<-state.transition(records=records, beta0=beta0,agem=agem[1:records],Nage_lookup=Nage_lookup, car_age=car_age[1:Tage], age_lookup = age_lookup[1:Nage_lookup])

  for (i in 1:records) {
    pos[i] ~ dbern(p[i])
  }

})

modelout <- nimbleModel(code= modelcode, constants = nimConsts, data = nimData,inits = nimInits) #runs okay, checks out
mcmcConf <- configureMCMC(modelout)#runs okay
mcmc <- buildMCMC(mcmcConf)#runs okay
Cmodel <- compileNimble(modelout,showCompilerOutput = TRUE)# this is where it breaks.

#####################################################################

Already suggested by Perry de Valpine, to just test a simple example, I was able to write and compile a simple nimble function:
hw <- nimbleFunction(run = function(){print("hello world")})
chw <- compileNimble(hw, showCompilerOutput = TRUE)

I have also previously successfully used a nimble function within a simple logistic regression model.

printErrors() from a nimbleMCMC call is maybe more informative:
P_5_modelcode_MID_5_nfCode.cpp: In member function ‘virtual void p_L5_UID_50::simulate(const indexedNodeInfo&) const’:
P_5_modelcode_MID_5_nfCode.cpp:851:80: error: invalid initialization of reference of type ‘NimArr<1, int>&’ from expression of type ‘NimArr<1, double>’
 Interm_106 = rcFun_5(20572, Interm_102, Interm_103, 132, Interm_104, Interm_105);
                                                                                ^
P_5_modelcode_MID_5_nfCode.cpp:769:20: note: in passing argument 3 of ‘NimArr<1, double> rcFun_5(int, double, NimArr<1, int>&, int, NimArr<1, double>&, NimArr<1, int>&)’
 NimArr<1, double>  rcFun_5 ( int ARG1_records_, double ARG2_beta0_, NimArr<1, int> & ARG3_agem_, int ARG4_Nage_lookup_, NimArr<1, double> & ARG5_car_age_, NimArr<1, int> & ARG6_age_lookup_ )  {
                    ^
At global scope:
cc1plus: warning: unrecognized command line option ‘-Wno-ignored-attributes’
cc1plus: warning: unrecognized command line option ‘-Wno-misleading-indentation’
make: *** [P_5_modelcode_MID_5_nfCode.o] Error 1

messages.body_plain:
Hi Alison,

Please try changing "agem = integer(1)" to "agem = double(1)", and the same for age_lookup, in the state.transition arguments.  All numbers in models are represented by double precision, even if they only make sense as integers. For scalars, this shouldn't matter (but you change integer(0) to double(0) as well), but for vectors it will matter.  The last error message you provided points in this direction.  I am not sure why it would work on one system and not on another, but please let us know if this fixes the problem.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Lokesh,

This same error message came up with another user in a recent post to
nimble-users. In that case the issue was
that for some set of values of the latent parameters and parameters
being optimized over, the log-likelihood calculation
returns NA or NaN or Inf or -Inf. At this point the expected
log-likelihood is not a finite numeric value and the optimization step
fails.

So my high-level suggestion is that you look and see if there are
latent parameter values that might be simulated
in the embedded MCMC or hyperparameter values that might be used by
the optimizer that would cause an NA/NaN/Inf/-Inf.
In particular think about parameter values on the boundary of finite
parameter ranges. It's possible that because of
numerical round-off error, the MCEM could produce parameter values
that to the computer are exactly on the boundary.

Another thing to look at is that in both calcZ and dCMP_nf  you should
probably work on the log scale as much
as possible for better numerical performance - multiplying and
dividing numbers can lead to numerical
overflow and underflow.

E.g. instead of:

prob <- pow((pow(lam, y)/factorial(y)),nu)/calcZ(lam, nu, sumTo)
      if(log) return(log(prob))
      else return(prob)

calculate the log prob directly and only exponentiate if the "log"
argument is TRUE.

Ideally NIMBLE's MCEM would do a better job trapping this situation
and returning helpful error message...

> nimble-users. In that case the issue was
> that for some set of values of the latent parameters and parameters
> being optimized over, the log-likelihood calculation
> returns NA or NaN or Inf or -Inf. At this point the expected
> log-likelihood is not a finite numeric value and the optimization step
> fails.
>
> So my high-level suggestion is that you look and see if there are
> latent parameter values that might be simulated
> in the embedded MCMC or hyperparameter values that might be used by
> the optimizer that would cause an NA/NaN/Inf/-Inf.
> In particular think about parameter values on the boundary of finite
> parameter ranges. It's possible that because of
> numerical round-off error, the MCEM could produce parameter values
> that to the computer are exactly on the boundary.
>
> Another thing to look at is that in both calcZ and dCMP_nf  you should
> probably work on the log scale as much
> as possible for better numerical performance - multiplying and
> dividing numbers can lead to numerical
> overflow and underflow.
>
> E.g. instead of:
>
> prob <- pow((pow(lam, y)/factorial(y)),nu)/calcZ(lam, nu, sumTo)
>       if(log) return(log(prob))
>       else return(prob)
>
> calculate the log prob directly and only exponentiate if the "log"
> argument is TRUE.
>
> Ideally NIMBLE's MCEM would do a better job trapping this situation
> and returning helpful error message...
>

messages.body_plain:
Zhihua, thanks for your usage of NIMBLE.  Unfortunately, I'm not able to re-create the error you mentioned ("Cannot iterate for parameter "ind")

I'm including my code below, slightly modified from your original, which runs fine for me, and the mixing / sampling appears to get off to a fine start (although I only ran it for 10,000 iterations).  The changes I made include:

-- Adding initial values for the b[1:159, 1:6] array, so that your model is fully initialized.
-- Changing from using nimbleMCMC(), to using the more modular and configurable workflow of using nimbleModel(), then configureMCMC(), buildMCMC(), and runMCMC().
-- Running for fewer iterations, and I skipped the thinning of the samples, but you can add that back in.

Anyway, it runs fine for me.  Please give this a try, and let us know if you still are having problems.

Which version of NIMBLE are you using?  It could perhaps be, that in older versions of NIMBLE, the dynamic indexing that you're using (with the "ind" variable) either wasn't implemented, or was "turned off" by default.  So you might consider trying to upgrade to NIMBLE version 0.7.2 available on CRAN.

Good luck!

Daniel

library(nimble)
library(mvtnorm)

S <- 159   # number of locations
X <- rmvnorm(159, sigma = diag(rep(1, 6)))
b1 <- rep(-1, S) + rnorm(S)
b2 <- rep(2, S) + rnorm(S)
b3 <- rep(0, S)
b4 <- rep(0, S)
b5 <- rep(2, S) + rnorm(S)
b6 <- rep(1, S) + rnorm(S)
y <- 1 + b1 * X[, 1] + b2 * X[, 2] + b3 * X[, 3] + b4 * X[, 4] + b5 * X[, 5] + b6 * X[, 6] + rnorm(S)

##(ii) spatial-specific coefficients
code <- nimbleCode({

    for (i in 1:S) {
        y[i] ~ dnorm(mu_y[i], tau = tau_y)
        mu_y[i] <-
            b0 + b[i, 1] * x1[i] + b[i, 2] * x2[i] +
            b[i, 3] * x3[i] + b[i, 4] * x4[i] + b[i, 5] * x5[i] + b[i, 6] * x6[i]
        b[i, 1:6] ~ dmnorm(mu_bm[1:6], cov = var_bm[1:6, 1:6])
    }
    var_bm[1:6, 1:6] <- diag(1/tau_bm[1:6])
    for (j in 1:6) {
        mu_bm[j] <- 0
        tau_bm[j] <- tau_bmm[ind[j] + 1]
        ind[j] ~ dbern(gamma[j])
        gamma[j] ~ dbeta(0.5, 0.5)
    }
    tau_bmm[1] <- tau_b0
    tau_bmm[2] <- tau_b0 * c
    b0 ~ dnorm(0, 1)
    tau_y ~ dgamma(1, 1)
})

constants <- list(S = 159, c = 0.0001, tau_b0 = 100)

data <- list(y = y, x1 = X[,1], x2 = X[,2], x3 =X[,3], x4 = X[,4], x5 = X[,5], x6 = X[,6])

inits <- list(tau_y = 1, tau_bm = rep(1,6), b0 = rnorm(1), ind = rep(1,6), gamma = runif(6),
              b = array(0, c(159,6)))   ## DT: added initial value for b array

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code, constants, data, inits)

## DT: calculate() returns a real number, model is fully initialized
Rmodel$calculate()

conf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel)

## check the sampler assignments.
## might consider whether or not you want the RW_block samplers assigned
## to each b[i, 1:6] ?
conf$printSamplers()

## add your monitors
conf$addMonitors(c("b0","b","ind","gamma","tau_y"))

Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(conf)

Cmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel)

set.seed(0)
samples <- runMCMC(Cmcmc, 10000)

samplesSummary(samples)

library(basicMCMCplots)
samplesPlot(samples, c('gamma', 'b0'))

#### this does the same thing:
##mcmc.out <- nimbleMCMC(code, constants, data, inits,
##                       monitors = c("b0","b","ind","gamma","tau_y"),
##                       niter = 50000, thin = 10, nchains = 1, setSeed = TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
I have been trying to convert a (slightly adapted) example from the BUGS Book to Nimble, but I don't think it is working as it should.

The basic idea is that we are fitting a normal distribution with known variance to six observed data points, and we have three which are unobserved but we know are greater than eight.

This is the code I am using:

code <- nimbleCode({
  for (i in 1:6) {y[i] ~ dnorm(mu, 1)}        # uncensored data

  ym[1]  ~ T(dnorm(mu,1), 8,)
  ym[2] ~ T(dnorm(mu,1), 8,)
  ym[3] ~  T(dnorm(mu,1), 8,)

  mu                   ~ dunif(0, 100)
})

data <- list(y = c(6,6,6,7,7,7), ym=c(NA,NA,NA))

inits <- list(mu = 7, ym = c(9,9,9))

mcmc.out <- nimbleMCMC(code = code,  data = data, inits = inits,  nchains = 2, niter = 100000, summary = TRUE, WAIC = TRUE,   monitors = c('mu', 'y', 'ym'))

However, what seems to be happening is that instead of finding the joint posterior of normal mean and three censored values, we are finding the posterior conditional only on the observed data, and imputing the censored values conditional on that (i.e., I would expect mu to be pulled up by the missing value estimates, but it is not):

> mcmc.out$summary$all.chains

y[2]  6.000000 6.000000 0.0000000  6.000000  6.000000

ym[3] 8.444607 8.335163 0.3958310  8.013012  9.471951

Any help here would be gratefully received.

messages.subject: Re: Censored data problem
messages.subject_clean: Censored data problem
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rob, good question.

By setting the initial values of 'ym' to NA, NIMBLE actually treats
them as parameters and not as data.
Since there is not a known value, so there is no way to have NIMBLE
treat 'ym' as data in the way you are trying to do it.
As a result, NIMBLE sees the 'ym' elements as unknowns with no
children and simply simulates into them given the current value of mu
at any
given iteration.

What you need here is to make sure to include the likelihood
contribution from the three censored values. You can think of these
as being Bernoulli with probability equal to the probability of being
greater than 8. In reality the data you observe really are
indicators of those values being bigger than 8, so that is what needs
to be coded in the model.

So you should be able to do something like this:

for(i in 1:3)
   ym[i] ~ dbern(pnorm(8, mu, 1, lower.tail = 0))  # note the
lower.tail argument needs to be numeric and not TRUE/FALSE
  # alternatively: ym[i] ~ dbern(1-pnorm(8, mu, 1))

data = list(ym = rep(1, 3), .....)

Per table 5.2.5 of the NIMBLE manual, if you use distribution
functions in model code or nimbleFunctions, only some the canonical
parameterizations (essentially those that R uses) are allowed so the
"1" here is the standard deviation. See also Section 11.2.4 of the
manual.

I haven't had the time to look more carefully at what BUGS and JAGS
would do in this case, but we modeled NIMBLE's handling of truncation
off of
what JAGS does, so I believe how one handles this in JAGS would be
along the lines of what I have above. But I could be wrong.

If anyone reading wants to weigh in on the comparison with BUGS and
JAGS for this sort of situation, please do!

-chris

messages.subject: Re: spike and slab prior for spatial-specific coefficients
messages.subject_clean: spike and slab prior for spatial-specific coefficients
messages.body_plain:
Hi Zhihua,

We've taken a more thorough look at this. The nimble code seems to be working as it should, but it looks like this model is not likely to mix much. As the model is written, in order to have a change in the status of an indicator variable, e.g. say from ind[3] = 0 (slab) to 1 (spike), all the corresponding  parameters b[, 3] should be *simultaneously* close to zero, which will be very rare.  Conversely, a move from the spike to the slab would be very unlikely because if all of the b[,3] parameters are close to zero, then the spike will have much higher probability than the slab.

We've more often seen spike and slab priors written with indicator variables that multiply coefficients, rather than modifying the variance (or precision) of the prior for the coefficients.  For example, one might write something like:

b0 + ind[1]*b[i, 1] * x1[i] + ... (similar for other coefficients).

So if an indicator variable is equal to zero, it also sets to zero the associated vector of coefficients; otherwise coefficients follow the slab distribution. Then the prior on the indicator variables' probability of being 1 is the probability of being in the slab.

Another approach would be to write custom samplers that could mix the indicator variables and coefficients jointly.  The "examples" tab at r-nimble.org <http://r-nimble.org/> shows an example with a reversible-jump sampler for a similar kind of problem. (We are working to make this more flexible and include it in nimble). See also Section 15.5 of the user manual which documents writing new samplers.

Best,

Sally

messages.body_plain:
Hi Lokesh,

I was finally able to get a bit of time to look more at your MCEM issue. It is indeed a numerical problem caused by not working on the log scale.
It's occurring when the optimization step puts values from the MCMC for the latent nodes into the model for the current set of values for the top level nodes
and the resulting model log probability is Inf or -Inf or NaN. In your case, because calcZ was not being done on the log scale, it was returning Inf or -Inf.
I've attached a version of your code (the code from your April 14 email) where key steps are done on the log scale (see everything where I made a comment noting "CHANGED").

The MCEM for the revised code now runs without the error. However, it takes a very long time to run/converge.

I'm also going to discuss with our development team some ideas so that when this sort of thing happens, we catch the Inf/-Inf/NaN that occurs in the calculation and
give the user more information about what has gone wrong.

Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am using the code below to fit my model. But every time I am getting at least 4 - 5 R_hat values > 1.1. Also is there option to check the convergence of our model at each iteration?

J = nlevels(Data_test$cate_var)

K = length(X_vars)
zero_vec_X = rep(0, K)
one_vec_X = rep(1, K)

nm.Data <- list(y_var = as.numeric(Data_test$y_var),
                Data_X = as.matrix(Data_test[, X_vars]),
                cate_var = as.numeric(Data_test$cate_var),
                S0 = diag(K) / (K + 2),
                zero_vec_X = zero_vec_X,
                constraint_X_bound = matrix(rep(1,J*K),J,K)
)

nm.Constants <- list(N = nrow(Data_test),
                     K = K,
                     J = J

)

######################### Parameters of Interest ################################################

nm.params <- c("alpha", "beta_X", "const")

######################### Initializations Function ##############################################

init_mu_X <- rtruncnorm(K, mean = 0, sd = 1, a = 0, b = 1)
init_Phi_X <- rwish((K+2), diag(K) * 0.01)
init_beta_X <- rtmvnorm(J, mean = zero_vec_X, sigma = (diag(K) * 0.5), lower = zero_vec_X, upper = one_vec_X, algorithm = "gibbs")

nm.inits <- list("alpha" = rtruncnorm(nlevels(Data_test$cate_var), mean = 10, sd = 1, a = 0, b = 15),
                 "mu_beta_X" = init_mu_X,
                 "Phi_X" = init_Phi_X,
                 "aux" = rgamma(1,1),
                 "beta_X" = init_beta_X

)

nm.Dimensions <- list(zero_vec_X = c(K),
                      mu_beta_X = c(K),
                      beta_X = c(J, K),
                      Sigma_X = c(K, K),
                      Sigma2_X = c(K, K),
                      Phi_X = c(K, K),
                      Phi1_X = c(K, K),
                      Phi2_X = c(K, K)
)

############################ Define Model #####################################################

nm.Code <- nimbleCode({

  ####################
  # Specify Likelihood
  ####################
  for (n in 1:N) {

    y_var[n] ~ dnorm ((alpha[cate_var[n]] + inprod(beta_X[cate_var[n], ] , Data_X[n, ])), tau)

  }

  for (j in 1:J) {
    for (m in 1:K) {
      constraint_X_bound[j,m] ~ dconstraint(0 < beta_X[j,m] & beta_X[j,m] <= 1)
    }
  }

  ################
  # Specify Priors
  ################

  # X_vars Priors

  for (j in 1:J) {

    beta_X[j, 1:K] ~ dmnorm(mean=mu_beta_X[], cov=Sigma_X[,])

    alpha[j] ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
  }

  # Error Prior
  aux ~ dgamma(0.001, 0.001)
  tau <- 1/aux

  ######################
  # Specify Hyper-Priors
  ######################
  Phi_X[1:K, 1:K] ~ dwish(S = S0[,], df = (K + 2)) #dinvwish(S = S0[,], df = (K+2))

  Sigma_X[1:K, 1:K] <- inverse(Phi_X[,])
  Sigma2_X[1:K, 1:K] <- Sigma_X[,]/0.01

  mu_beta_X[1:K] ~ dmnorm(zero_vec_X[], Sigma2_X[,])

})

############################# Build  model ############################################

set.seed(1234)
nm.Model <- nimbleModel(code=nm.Code, constants=nm.Constants, dimensions = nm.Dimensions,
                        data=nm.Data, inits=nm.inits, check = F, calculate = TRUE)

#pumpMCEM <- buildMCEM(model = nm.Model, latentNodes = c("aux", "Phi_X","mu_beta_X"), boxConstraints = list())

#pumpMLE <- pumpMCEM$run()

nm.Compiled <- compileNimble(nm.Model, showCompilerOutput = FALSE)
nm.Conf <- configureMCMC(nm.Model, print = TRUE)

nm.Conf$addMonitors(c("alpha", "beta_X"))

nm.MCMC <- buildMCMC(nm.Conf, enableWAIC = TRUE)

nm.ConfMCMC <- compileNimble(nm.MCMC, showCompilerOutput = F , project = nm.Model)

chains =2
nm.fit <- runMCMC(nm.ConfMCMC, niter = 100e3, nburnin = 30e3, inits = nm.inits, nchains = chains,
                  setSeed = T, samples = T, summary = TRUE, WAIC = TRUE)

tmp <- nm.fit$summary$all.chains
nm.fit$WAIC

r_hat = NULL

for(i in rownames(tmp)){
  mcmc_samples <- NULL
  for(j in 1:chains){
    samples_chain <- nm.fit$`samples`[[j]]
    mcmc_samples <- cbind(mcmc_samples, samples_chain[, i])
  }
  colnames(mcmc_samples) <- names(nm.fit$`samples`)
  r_hat <- rbind(r_hat, cbind(i, R.hat(mcmc_samples)))
}
r_hat <- data.frame(r_hat)
names(r_hat) <- c("name", "R_hat")

r_hat$R_hat <- as.numeric(as.character(r_hat$R_hat))
length(which(r_hat$R_hat >= 1.1))
